Five rivers braid down through the shires to meet at the Confluence, and the greatest of them, the Miskatonic, runs through the center of the farms before it reaches the city, carrying barges, timber, and the occasional smuggled thing.
What follows are the six settlements a city person is most likely to have heard of, and most likely to have heard wrong:

body.li: ​ Whittington: The southernmost settlement of any size, Whittington is a logging town on the

body.p: County's ragged southern edge, where the shire valleys give out into the disputed scrub that nobody has ever bothered to survey precisely because there is nothing there worth the surveyor's fee. It exists to cut, mill, and float timber, and its several hundred residents are the sort of people who can drop a two-hundred-foot redwood in the direction they intend and think nothing of it. It is a hard, close, capable town that settles its own disputes.

body.li: ​ Steel Point: This town is driven into the mountain range Aldenmere makes the beginning of,

body.p: Steel Point is where it means it. Steel Point is the largest settlement in the County outside the city, and it does nothing but dig, following the iron and copper down into the dark under the range on a schedule set by the freight contracts, and the town's whole rhythm is the shift whistle, the cage, and the long climb back to daylight. The Spencer Industrial Group owns the principal mines, most of the stores, most of the housing, and the loyalty or resentment of nearly everyone in the town, and the family functions as Steel Point's de-facto government, convenient for the dominion and complicated for the miners. Lucas Spencer's word is law here more reliably than any law is. The work is well-paid by County standards and lethal by any other, and the town keeps its own hard counsel.

body.li: ​ Ipswitch: Past Steel Point the road climbs on, worsening, through the high passes, and where

body.p: it finally gives up, it arrives at a village of perhaps fifty souls. It exists because the road had to stop somewhere and this is where it stopped. It is the last inhabited place before the range becomes only rock and weather, and its people raise animals such as sheep and goats on the thin high pasture, a few hardy cattle, the wool and mutton and milk that come down the mountain in the same carts that carry ore, when the passes are open, which is not all year.

Ipswitch keeps to itself. Fifty people at the top of a mountain in the winter become, of necessity, a single stubborn organism, married and remarried into a handful of surnames, keeping traditions the lowland shires abandoned generations ago and calendars the city has never heard of. They are hospitable to travelers in the hard, obligatory way, and are unforthcoming about a great many things.

body.li: ​ Brancrug: This town sits in the geographic middle of the County. It is a crossroads town

body.p: where the roads to Whittington, to Mystic, and on toward Ingfell all pass through or branch apart, and it has made a modest, comfortable living for generations as a reliable stop before those roads get lonely. It has good pubs, more of them than its resident population justifies, a coaching inn or two updated with a petrol pump, working farms, and a scatter of middling gentry estates whose families are grand enough to be somebody in Brancrug and nobody at all in Aldenmere (or a summer home of an Aldenmere family). Nothing of importance has ever happened in Brancrug. Everyone traveling the County's interior stops there, refuels there, drinks there, and talks there, and a patient listener in the right pub on the right evening can learn the movements of half the County without leaving the fireplace.

body.li: ​ Mystic: Set in the heart of the shire farmland on the bank of the Miskatonic, Mystic is the

body.p: distribution point for a wide spread of farmhouses and smallholdings too scattered to supply themselves directly from Vallam. The trucks and the river barges come up from the city and drop their loads of seed, feed, tools, fuel, wire, parts, and another hundred things a working farm runs through, and the outlying farmers come in to Mystic to buy, collect, and haul the rest of the way home themselves. A busy lil’ town, with warehouses, a feed store, a chandlery, and a wharf where the barges tie up. You can hire a hand here, sell a crop, hear who has died and who is selling up, and quietly arrange the sort of transaction that does not want the city's paperwork.

body.li: ​ Ingfell: A substantial coastal town on the far shore, well away from the city's stretch of the

body.p: Eye, and the hardest of all six to actually reach. The roads to Ingfell are poorly kept and, past Brancrug, poorly marked: signposts that should direct a traveler toward the town are missing, or turned, or were apparently never erected, and within the town itself the street signs have been quietly removed, so that an outsider trying to find a specific address discovers that no one seems able, or willing, to help them do it. A first-time visitor can find sagging wharves, shuttered frontages, salt-eaten paint, a harbor that clearly once did far more business than it does now. It is a town that has no public library, no chamber of commerce, no civic apparatus of the kind every other settlement its size maintains, and does not appear to feel the lack. There is a look to certain of the old Ingfell lines, something in the set of the eyes, the skin, the neck, the gait, that the town treats as unremarkable, and it runs in the families that never leave and never marry out. Vallam, for its part, has decided that Ingfell is a depressed and inbred fishing backwater best left to itself, and files the occasional strange report from that stretch of coast under nothing at all.
A categorical guide to the institutions, societies, families, and enterprises that shape life in the Vallam of 1926.

children.title: The Vallam Metropolitan Police Department

body.p: The Vallam Metropolitan Police Department (VMPD) is divided into eight precincts loosely aligned with the city's major neighborhoods. The Central Precinct, located in the Sovereign Quarter, serves as headquarters. Commissioner Arthur Voss, a career administrator, has managed the department through Prohibition by maintaining a careful distinction between what he knows and what he officially chooses to ignore.

The VMPD's relationship with Vallam's criminal underworld varies by precinct, ranging from active enforcement cooperation to near-total institutional capture. The Prohibition Division operates within the VMPD's structure but reports directly to the national Home Office, creating resentment throughout the regular force. Relations between the two bodies are strained, and inter-agency cooperation is minimal.

meta: Central Precinct: The Sovereign Quarter

children.title: The Prohibition Division

body.p: Formed under the National Prohibition Act of 1924, the Prohibition Division enforces national alcohol restrictions as the enforcement arm of the Temperance Bureau. Its officers are recruited primarily from outside the regular police force, which was considered too compromised to enforce Prohibition reliably. The Division excels at high-profile raids, prominent bootlegger arrests, and major shipment seizures but struggles with routine enforcement due to its officers' lack of established neighborhood relationships.

The Division is headed by Chief Agent Emmeline Strauch, a former customs investigator known for her competence and blunt manner. Recognizing that the VMPD ranges from indifferent to openly hostile toward her mandate, she has developed independent networks of informants and contacts outside its structure. Commissioner Voss finds these arrangements deeply irritating.

meta: Location: Millfield, a deliberately unremarkable building on Crane Street

children.title: The Suppression Bureau

body.p: The Suppression Bureau operates covertly within the Dominion government under the official designation Office for Cultural and Historical Integrity, a deliberately vague title that has concealed its true mandate for thirty years. The Bureau manages the boundary between the ordinary world and the supernatural, restricting exposure to phenomena and knowledge that can endanger those who encounter them.

Its primary functions include: the censorship and removal of written, artistic, and printed works that describe, reference, or inadvertently replicate knowledge of the horrors; the investigation and, if necessary, the disappearance of individuals who have come into contact with supernatural entities or knowledge and represent a risk of further exposure or contamination; the monitoring of organisations and individuals with demonstrated occult interest; and the containment of what the Bureau's internal documents call threshold events. These refer to occurrences in which the boundary between the ordinary and the supernatural has been breached in ways that require immediate and deniable management.

The Bureau's agents carry badges whose statement reads Aliis Si Licet, Tibi Non Licet, which can translate to “What is permitted for others is not permitted for you”, a quotation selected by the Bureau's founder. Agents receive only enough information to perform their assigned duties and are discouraged from investigating the broader mandate. The Bureau maintains that restricted knowledge protects agents from psychological harm, a rationale that is partly justified and partly convenient.

Director Zachary Wakefield, forty-one, heads the Vallam Station. His background before joining the Bureau is undocumented in any files accessible to his agents. He rarely leaves the Sovereign Quarter building; when he does, observers take notice and question what prompted his departure. The Bureau cooperates with St. Butcher's Custos when operationally necessary and surveys the Hush House, the University's Society for the Exploration of the Unexplained, and several individuals connected to the Eclipsiad's surviving underground presence. People disappear from Vallam regularly, and some would likely remain had the Bureau not needed them to.

meta: Location: Officially listed as a division of the Home Ministry, physically located in a four-story building in the Sovereign Quarter that is not labeled and has no public-facing signage beyond a street number.

children.title: The Dominion Naval Command

body.p: Headquartered at a large complex on the Merchant District's northern waterfront, adjacent to the naval dockyards. The Navy is present in Vallam as a major institutional fact of the city's life. Its dockyards employ several thousand civilian workers, its officers occupy a significant portion of the Aldenmere lower-slope residences, and its command structure is one of the city's most important centres of power. Admiral Constance Harrow, the first woman to hold the position, appointed in 1923 after a career that included the most successful anti-smuggling operation in Dominion naval history and the management of the Selkeff Straits monitoring station during the early war years, is one of the most significant people in Vallam and one of the least publicly prominent, which she considers an appropriate arrangement.

meta: Location: A large complex on the Merchant District's northern waterfront, adjacent to the naval dockyards.

children.title: The Vallam Standard

body.p: The Standard is the Dominion's newspaper of record. The broadsheet that foreign governments read to understand what Fairbourne thinks, that Parliament reads to understand what the public thinks, and that the public reads to understand what Parliament is doing wrong. It has been publishing continuously since 1801 and has, over that period, broken more significant stories than any other paper on the Reach, retracted fewer of them than any reasonable person would expect, and been the target of more legal threats than all other Vallam newspapers combined.

Its editor-in-chief, Barnabas Quelch, is seventy-one, has been at the Standard for forty-three years, holds views that cannot be mapped onto any recognisable political position without significant distortion, and has an editorial instinct that his reporters find terrifying and his proprietors find, with some justice, more valuable than the building they publish from. The Standard's relationship with the Suppression Bureau is contentious. The Bureau has successfully suppressed four Standard stories in the last decade. The Standard is, in all four cases, aware that the suppression occurred.

meta: A six-story building in Millfield, whose printing presses are audible from the street during night runs.

children.title: The Vallam Evening Courier

body.p: The Standard's principal competitor for serious news coverage, younger by forty years, considerably more willing to pursue stories through methods the Standard's code of ethics does not endorse, and consistently better at the kind of crime reporting that requires sources in the criminal community.

Its crime desk is staffed primarily by former police officers and one former bootlegger whose arrangement with the Courier's editor has never been formally documented. Its editor, Petra Daun, is forty-four, was the Courier's crime reporter for fifteen years before being given the chair, and has a network of informants across Vallam's underworld that several law enforcement agencies would describe as inappropriately comprehensive if they were willing to acknowledge officially that they know about it.

meta: Location: The Narrows, Southgate Building

children.title: The Morning Post

body.p: The Morning Post is not the Standard or the Courier. It knows it is not the Standard or the Courier, and it has made a consistent editorial decision that the correct response to this is to be more useful to the people who actually read it rather than to the people who do not. It covers Vallam's neighborhoods with greater granularity than either of its larger competitors. Local council votes, school board appointments, street-level crime, the kind of community news that the Standard considers beneath notice and the Courier considers insufficiently dramatic. Its readership is Ashford and Ironside and Fenwick. Its journalists are from those neighborhoods and know them in ways that no desk at Millfield or the Narrows can replicate. It breaks local stories that the Standard then follows up on at three times the space and half the accuracy.

meta: Headquartered in ashford, a functional brick building on the high street

children.title: Illustrated Gazette

body.p: A weekly periodical combining long-form journalism, cultural criticism, and illustration. Its arts coverage is the best in the city. Its political coverage takes the form of long essays that are read by the people who write them, the people who disagree with them, and not many others. Its editor, Marguerite Palliser, is a former academic who treats the Gazette as an ongoing argument with the city about what matters, and whose back-page column, weekly, unsigned, and written in a style that makes it instantly identifiable, has been both prosecuted for libel twice and nominated for the Dominion's press award four times. She lost both trials and won two nominations

meta: Situated in Greenvale near the university

children.title: Vallam Chamber of Commerce

body.p: The Chamber is the city's primary business advocacy body, formally voluntary, practically indispensable for any commercial operation that wants a voice in city policy, licensing decisions, or the various municipal processes that govern commercial life in Vallam. Its membership ranges from the large Aldenmere holding companies to the shopkeepers of Coppergate, though the Chamber's governance structure, a board elected by members weighted by contribution tier, means that in practice the large interests tend to set the agenda and the small ones attend the quarterly meetings and vote accordingly.

The current Chamber president is Duncan Crayle, the managing director of a mid-sized shipping insurance firm whose career has been built on knowing more about who needs what than anyone else in the room. Crayle is not corrupt but deeply well-informed, which produces similar outcomes in many situations. The Chamber's relationship with the city's criminal enterprises is mostly transactional and mostly conducted at arm's length. A number of the Chamber's members operate legitimate businesses that are adjacent to illegitimate supply chains, and the Chamber has a consistent institutional policy of not asking questions whose answers would require it to do something.

meta: Location: Millfield, Commerce House, a large Edwardian building with a public meeting room that can seat three hundred.

children.title: Rotary Club

body.p: Vallam's Rotary chapter was founded in 1912 by a group of younger professionals who found the Chamber of Commerce too formal and the established clubs too expensive, and wanted an organization focused on doing something useful rather than simply knowing useful people. The current membership is largely drawn from the working professional class, teachers, junior lawyers, small business owners, mid-grade civil servants, with a higher proportion of women than any of the other civic organisations and a younger average age than all of them.

The Rotary's service projects in 1926 include a reading program in Ironside's primary schools, a weekly soup provision operation in Coppergate, and an ongoing campaign to get the city council to finally address Fenwick's drainage problem. None of these projects are glamorous, but they are all doing something. The club's president, Vera Ashby, is a secondary school teacher at Ashford Comprehensive who runs the organisation with a cheerful relentlessness that its members find either inspiring or exhausting depending on the week and how many service hours they have had to log.

meta: Location: Ashford, meeting weekly at the Ashford Arms public house (currently serving what the landlord describes as a selection of non-alcoholic fermented beverages)

children.title: The Masonic Lodge. Charter No. 7

body.p: The Masonic Lodge has been operating in Vallam since 1788, long enough that its membership rolls read as a partial history of the city's professional and academic establishment. Its rituals, so far as the public knows anything about them, involve a mixture of ceremonial tradition, fraternal obligation, and a system of moral philosophy expressed through symbolic architecture that members take more seriously than outsiders tend to expect.

Its secrets, which are genuinely kept, are less dramatic than popular imagination suggests and more practical. The lodge's membership overlaps extensively with the city's judiciary, its senior civil service, and its major financial institutions, and the fraternal obligation of the lodge produces a network of informal professional support and mutual assistance that operates quietly and effectively. The Master of the Lodge is Sir Edmund Bracke, a retired judge whose post-retirement social life is conducted almost entirely through the lodge's structures.

The Companion Circle, an informal associate group for women, acknowledged but formally separate from the lodge, meets monthly in a private room at the Grand Peeress Hotel. It does not include the lodge's ritual elements and has a considerably more overtly social character. Several of its members have been attempting for ten years to formalize the association into something with actual lodge status. This effort is proceeding in the way that such efforts proceed inside institutions that would prefer them not to succeed.

meta: Location: Millfield, a building on Redfield Street that is distinguished from its neighbors primarily by the absence of any signage whatsoever.

children.title: Vallam Athletic Association

body.p: The VAA is the city's central sports and socialising club for those who want the social infrastructure of an athletic association without the commitment to regular athletic activity. Its membership includes genuine sportspeople, such as the the Rowing Club, the Amateur Boxing League, and a Cricket Association that takes itself seriously, plus a substantially larger contingent who joined for the discounted bar, the connections, and the general pleasure of belonging to something whose atmosphere smells of liniment and old leather without having to exert themselves. Both constituencies are welcome, and the VAA's success as an institution derives largely from this inclusive approach.

Its facilities include a gymnasium, a swimming pool, several dining rooms, a bar, a billiard hall, and a room informally designated as the smoking lounge in which no smoking has technically been possible since the incident of 1919, the nature of which is not recorded in the official minutes. The President, Captain (Ret.) Frederick Orme, is a former army officer whose definition of sport expands conveniently to include most of what the VAA's members actually want to do there.

meta: Location: A large Victorian building in Greenvale, adjacent to the University sports grounds, known simply as the VAA House.

children.title: The Society for the Exploration of the Unexplained

body.p: The SEU began in 1919 as a response to a wave of interest among returning veterans and their younger university counterparts in ghost stories, paranormal reports from the front, and the general sense that the world, having demonstrated its willingness to be much stranger and more horrible than expected, might also be strange in more interesting ways. Its membership is drawn from the University's more socially peripheral students. The ones who find the mainstream student social world slightly impenetrable and prefer a context in which enthusiasm for strange subjects is a social asset rather than a liability.

The SEU investigates reported paranormal events in Vallam with the rigour available to a group of undergraduates who have read a lot but have little field experience. Their investigations are almost uniformly unsuccessful in finding genuine evidence of anything supernatural, which is partly because the city's actual supernatural activity is well enough concealed that undergraduate investigators won't stumble onto it by accident, and partly because the SEU's investigative methodology, while enthusiastic, is not sophisticated. Several of its members are, however, more observant than average, and the SEU's archive of reported strange occurrences in Vallam, five years of case files, compiled with inconsistent but genuine diligence, contains, buried in the less dramatic material, several reports that the Suppression Bureau has reason to wish it had found before the SEU did.

The faculty advisor, Dr. Clement Foss, teaches in the Esoteric Studies faculty and is broadly supportive of the SEU in the sense that he signs the paperwork required for them to exist as a university society and does not attend their meetings. He is aware of considerably more than the SEU's members and has made a careful decision about how much of that awareness to share.

meta: Location: University of Vallam, a borrowed basement room beneath the Esoteric Studies building, meetings Wednesday evenings

children.title: The Vallam Ladies' Shooting Club

body.p: Officially registered as a marksmanship sports society under the University's athletics programme, the VLSC is, in practice, a government-sponsored recruitment pipeline for the Dominion's Women's Auxiliary Corps, which has been accepting female volunteers into non-combat military roles since 1917 and combat-adjacent roles since 1922, and which has been trying to do both of these things without making it obviously a military recruitment operation since a Public Conscription Debate in 1924. The Club's official patron is the University's Athletics Department. Its practical administration is managed by a liaison from the Dominion War Ministry whose university affiliation is described, on all relevant paperwork, as visiting instructor in applied athletics.

The Club's membership includes women who genuinely want to learn to shoot, women who have intuited or been quietly told about the military connection and want to join the war effort, women who think it is funny that the Dominion's military recruitment is happening in a university shooting club basement, and one woman, Sergeant Instructor Ilara Vetch (university paperwork: Miss Vetch, Instructor), who has been running the Club since 1921 and whose combat record from the Corda front is significantly more extensive than her title suggests. The firing range is in use most evenings and all day Saturday and Sunday. The walls are thick enough to be effectively soundproofed.
Sergeant-Instructor Vetch has made this point to University administration on several occasions when other building use has been proposed.

meta: University of Vallam, the Pennant Building, with a fully soundproofed firing range in the basement

children.title: The St. Aldrek's Club

body.p: The St. Aldrek's Club is, formally, a private members' club for students, alumni and senior staff of St.

Aldrek's College, offering dining, reading rooms, overnight accommodation for visiting alumni, and the specific institutional feeling of a place whose purpose is to allow its members to be unavailable. Its building has been modified over the decades to eliminate window sight lines from the street, to install a rear entrance accessible without passing through the main lobby, and to soundproof, with considerable thoroughness, its private dining rooms.

These modifications were funded by the Club's membership and are not mentioned in its official prospectus. Within the Club's structure, the most significant and least officially acknowledged entity is the Aldrek Skulls, the Club's senior fraternity, whose membership is invitation-only, whose meetings are conducted in a room that non-members do not know exists, and whose influence in the placement of St. Aldrek's graduates into positions in law, finance, and the civil service has been the subject of four separate Standard investigations, none of which produced enough documentation to publish. The Skulls are not sinister in any supernatural sense. They are sinister in the ordinary sense of being a group of men with institutional connections and significant mutual interest in each other's continued success, operating without accountability.

The Skulls' current chair is Reginald Vacarro, a property lawyer whose office in Millfield represents a portfolio of clients whose legal needs occasionally require the kind of discretion that the Skulls' network is specifically equipped to provide.

meta: A converted townhouse on Fenwick's main residential street, three buildings from the St. Aldrek's College eastern gate

children.title: Vallam Amateur Theatre Company

body.p: The VATC is one of Vallam's oldest continuously operating amateur artistic institutions, founded in 1887 by a group of civil servants who found that government work, while intellectually satisfying, offered insufficient opportunity for melodrama. It has since become the primary social institution for a particular cross-section of the city: people who work in professional occupations during the day and want, in the evenings, to be someone else entirely. Its membership includes accountants, lawyers, teachers, a surprising number of police officers, and at least three individuals whose day occupation is of sufficient sensitivity that their VATC membership is the main thing their colleagues know about their personal lives.

The Company produces four shows per year from a mixture of established works, original productions, and the occasional experiment that the Committee describes as ambitious and the audience describes as testing, in The Lamp Room's intimate 180-seat house. Backstage at The Lamp Room is one of the more reliable social environments in Vallam. The greenroom is never empty, the caretaker serves tea at all hours without being asked, and the Company's tradition of post-show suppers at the restaurant next door has continued without interruption since 1891, including during the recent years of the Prohibition Act during which the restaurant's wine list became, officially, a menu of grape-based restorative beverages.

The Company's director is Sylvester Quine, a former professional actor who had a respectable provincial career before returning to Vallam and discovering that he preferred directing amateurs to performing with professionals, because amateurs are doing it because they love it, and that turns out to matter. He is also one of the more reliable sources in the city for information about who is having an affair with whom, a fact that several parties value for different reasons.

meta: The Terrace, a converted former music hall called The Lamp Room, leased from the city at rates that the City Council reviews annually and consistently fails to raise

children.title: First Ladies of Vallam

body.p: The First Ladies are not exactly a formal organisation. They are a social network with an identity, defined by shared ancestry, shared wealth, and a shared decision that the constraints society places on women of their position are less binding than those women are generally led to believe. Membership requires either a demonstrable Vallam lineage traceable to colonial-era settlement, a documented family presence in the city of three or more generations, or sufficient wealth and the endorsement of three existing members, which in practice means that the society is roughly equally divided between old money who earned their membership through birth and new money who earned it through the right combination of charming the right people.

The First Ladies have a reputation in Vallam that they are “aware of, have largely decided to cultivate, and consider to be, on balance, more accurate than their critics would prefer to acknowledge”. They are louder, more present, and more comfortable in spaces traditionally dominated by men than the social conventions of 1926 technically endorse. Several of them are genuinely talented musicians and performers; the nucleus of the group grew from a shared interest in jazz and the social world that surrounded it, and that connection to the music and the clubs remains central to the First Ladies' character.

Their informal leader  (the First Ladies have no formal leadership, but there is a person whose preferences shape what the group does) is Adeline Fairchild, twenty-eight, a member of the Fairchild branch of the Fairbourne family offshoot network, who plays the piano with a technical accomplishment she consistently refuses to take seriously and whose social influence extends far further than she typically allows people to know she is exerting it.

meta: Nominally, wherever they happen to be. In practice, The Terrace hotels, the Confluence clubs, the speakeasies of the Narrows, and various private residences across Aldenmere

children.title: Hush House

body.p: The Hush House Society presents itself, to the limited extent that it presents itself to anything outside its membership, as a society devoted to esoteric philosophy, alchemical study, and the collection of rare books. This presentation is accurate. It is also incomplete.

The Society was founded in 1889 by Desmond Farrant, an independently wealthy antiquarian whose collection of pre-Astralist texts represented, at the time of his death in 1911, one of the most comprehensive private occult libraries on the Reach. The manor he used as its headquarters, Hush House, on Strand Isle, a building whose peculiar acoustic qualities give it a permanent hushed quality that visitors invariably note and cannot explain, passed to the Society rather than to Farrant's family, a provision of his will that his family contested unsuccessfully for several years.

The current Society numbers thirty-one members, drawn from Vallam's professional and artistic upper-middle class. Most of them understand themselves to be members of a sophisticated intellectual club with excellent library access and a pleasingly theatrical approach to its own meetings. Some of them have noticed that the library's deeper stacks contain texts that are not catalogued and that produce, in extended reading, a specific kind of headache and a tendency to see things in peripheral vision. A very small number have noticed that the headache is not the worst thing the texts can produce.

The Society's current chair is Theodora Clemens, a retired chemist who joined in 1914 and has spent the twelve years since moving carefully and methodically through the library's uncatalogued section, recording what she finds, and reaching conclusions that she has not shared with any of the Society's other members. She is sixty-seven, moves slowly, asks precise questions, and has not been unwell in fourteen years, which she attributes to a good diet.

meta: Strand Isle, in a large Victorian manor known as Hush House, accessible by private ferry from the southern Merchant District docks

children.title: The Vallam Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals

body.p: The VSPCA was founded in 1891 and has operated as an entirely conventional animal welfare organisation for most of its history, running Vallam's only animal shelter, advocating for animal welfare legislation, and prosecuting cruelty cases through civil channels. Its current membership is approximately two hundred, with a core volunteer group of around thirty who do the actual work.

The organisation's unofficial mascot and most significant asset, in terms of public attention, is a family of five red pandas that arrived in Vallam in 1921 aboard a diplomatic vessel from a Renascia-aligned state, as part of a gift shipment to a private collector who subsequently went bankrupt and lost them to creditors. The VSPCA acquired them through a city auction, built a suitable enclosure in its garden, and discovered that the public's appetite for visiting the organisation's premises increased by approximately 400% immediately thereafter. The eldest and largest of the five, a round, placid animal named Cohh who has achieved the status of local celebrity, is the most photographed resident of Vallam after the King and is generally acknowledged by the organisation's members to be responsible for a significant percentage of its annual donations.

meta: Greenvale, a converted Victorian house three blocks from the University hospital, with a large garden that has been modified to serve as an animal welfare facility

children.title: Vallam Gun Club

body.p: The Vallam Gun Club occupies a position in Aldenmere's social ecosystem somewhere between a sporting society and a private members' club that has chosen firearms as its organising rationale. Its membership is drawn from the Aldenmere wealthy with a minority of enthusiasts from Greenvale and Millfield who have been admitted through the standard introduction process and who have learned that the Gun Club's social functions, monthly dinners, annual shooting competition (whose prizes are disproportionate to the competition's actual prestige), and informal gatherings on the practice range that last longer than practice ranges ordinarily warrant, are its primary purpose and the shooting is the justification.

The Club is owned and operated by Horatio Parrington, the proprietor of Parrington's on Ironside Street, Vallam's most comprehensively stocked firearms retailer, which serves both the professional and the sporting market with equal accommodation. Parrington is sixty-three, compact, with the specific physique of someone who has handled precision instruments all his life, and possesses a conversational style that produces, in people who underestimate him, the gradual discovery that they have told him considerably more than they intended to. He is not affiliated with any criminal organisation and knows about most of them, because they buy from him, and Parrington has a policy of excellent memory and no questions.

meta: Below the Aldenmere Golf Course, on the mountain's east face, in a long timber-and-stone building accessible by a road that is not on any city map and which gun club members simply know

children.title: The Ecdysis Society

body.p: The Ecdysis Society is a performance and dance collective that is, in the city's broader cultural consciousness, simultaneously famous and impossible to describe accurately to anyone who hasn't been. It is known (imprecisely) through the accounts of those who have attended, as a dance club, a performance space, a sensory experience, something to do with transformation, something to do with shedding, something that you are told about by a friend who attended and who struggles to explain exactly what they saw, only that they watched it for what felt like twenty minutes and left at three in the morning.

It is run by Amavasya Hessenger, a woman whose background is not clearly established in any source that anyone has been able to verify. She is tall and bright-eyed in a way that suggests either exceptional health or the permanent presence of something being very interested in everything around her. She blinks infrequently. The Society's logo on the door, membership cards and brooches worn by the performers is a moth. The performers of the Ecdysis Society are extraordinary. What they do varies each month, shaped by Hessenger's direction and the dynamic of the audience and performers present.

meta: The Narrows, in a building that is not findable without knowing which door to push and which painted number to ignore.
Opens only on nights of the full moon.

children.title: St. Butcher's Cathedral (The Main Congregation)

body.p: St. Butcher's is Vallam's largest and most prominent Lysterist cathedral, the seat of the Bishop of Vallam and the primary place of worship for the city's Lysterist majority. Its choir school, its charitable programmes, and its social presence in Ironside and the surrounding neighborhoods make it one of the city's significant civic institutions in addition to its religious function. The Bishop, Aldous Maren, is seventy-six, scholarly, theologically sophisticated, and genuinely uncertain about several things that his position officially requires certainty about. He is also one of the more perceptive readers of character in Vallam, which makes him interesting to a wider range of people than his age and position might suggest.

meta: Ironside, occupying a full city block on the neighborhood's central street

children.title: St. Butcher's Custos

body.p: The Custos is publicly described as a Classical Astralist outreach ministry of St. Butcher's, focused on practical community service and pastoral care across Vallam's neighborhoods.

The Custos was established in 1847 following an event in the Narrows that the official cathedral record describes as “an episode of civil disorder requiring pastoral response” and that Custos internal records describe in considerably more specific and alarming terms. Since then, the Custos has operated as what is essentially an ecclesiastical rapid response capability for supernatural incursion: a small group of trained individuals, drawn primarily from the cathedral's clergy and lay members, who are aware of the nature of the world's darker inhabitants and who maintain a body of procedural knowledge, about how to manage the consequences of encounters with them.

The Custos's training includes practical components that would surprise the cathedral's general congregation, and its small library includes texts that the Suppression Bureau is intermittently interested in and consistently unable to remove, partly because removing them from church property raises jurisdictional issues and partly because the Custos's senior membership tends to inexplicably know they're coming.

The Custos operates approximately twenty active members in 1926, organised in small response teams under the leadership of Father Billy Callum, a former military chaplain whose tour in the Corda campaign exposed him to things that field chaplaincy training had not prepared him for and that led, through a sequence of events he does not enjoy describing, to his current position. He is forty-four and has a relationship with the Suppression Bureau that is best described as mutually reluctant professional cooperation.

meta: St. Butcher's Cathedral, operating from the chapter house's lower level, which has two rooms that are kept locked and are not on the cathedral's floor plan

children.title: Fairchild Family

body.p: The Fairchilds are the most prominent of Fairbourne's bastard offshoot branches, descendants of a liaison between the third Fairbourne monarch's younger brother and a Cerani merchant's daughter in the mid-1600s, legitimised by a patent of nobility that is slightly more complicated to explain than the family's social position requires, and which the family accordingly does not explain unless directly asked. They have been in Aldenmere for a century and a half, and they have been collecting owls for most of it.

Fairchild House has a number of facilities housing over forty owls, actual pets of the family's members current patriarch, Cornelius Fairchild, fifty-eight, who believes that owls are the intellectually most honest animals. Predators who make no pretence of being anything else, and who are more perceptive than their stillness suggests. This is, those who know Cornelius observe, a reasonable description of the man himself.

His daughter Adeline Fairchild (see: First Ladies of Vallam) is the family member most visible in the city's social life. His son and heir Edmund Fairchild, thirty-one, manages the family's various investment interests from an office in Millfield and is widely considered to be quietly becoming more significant than his present profile suggests.

meta: Upper Aldenmere, Fairchild House, a large late-Georgian property notable for the owl motif that appears consistently across its architectural details, carved into the gateposts, rendered in the ironwork of the balcony, present in the family's monogram. They are the family's most consistent personality trait, expressed in stone.

children.title: Harwick-Sel Family

body.p: The Harwick-Sels are a merged family line produced by the marriage in 1876 of the Harwick banking family and the Sel shipping concern, explicitly arranged by both families' patriarchs for commercial reasons and has produced, in subsequent generations, both genuine affection and excellent return on investment. The family's current head is Lyra Harwick-Sel, fifty-nine, who inherited the combined enterprise after the deaths of both her husband and her father within eighteen months of each other in 1907, made a practical decision to manage both concerns as a single entity, and has spent the seventeen years since demonstrating that this was the right decision. She sits on the Vallam Chamber of Commerce board, the University of Vallam Court, and the advisory board of the Dominion Naval Command, whose last position is entirely appropriate given that the Harwick-Sel shipping concern holds three current naval supply contracts.

meta: Mid-Aldenmere, Harwick Hall, a Victorian Gothic property whose tower is the most visible silhouette on Aldenmere's slope after the Golf Course.

children.title: Calloway Family

body.p: The Calloways are a legal family. Four consecutive generations of barristers, solicitors, and at least one judge, whose current representative, Sir Gerald Calloway, sixty-two, sits on the Dominion Appeals Court and whose connection to Vallam's Masonic Lodge is well-known to its membership and politely unacknowledged outside it. The family's more interesting current member is his niece, Helena Calloway, twenty-nine, who graduated from the University of Vallam Law Faculty in 1919, one of the first batch of women to complete the degree, and has spent the six years since building a practice that specialises in cases that other firms decline. She is effective, her fees are not modest, and she has a client list that includes several individuals whose presence in a respectable law practice requires explanation that she does not provide.

meta: Lower Aldenmere, Calloway Terrace, a row of four adjoining townhouses purchased by the family across three generations and opened into a continuous residence without obvious exterior alteration

children.title: Spencer House

body.p: The Spencers are industrialists. Not the old-money kind who made their fortune three generations ago and have since been living on the principal, but the working kind who are still making it and are not entirely finished. Lucas Spencer, fifty-five, is the family's current head: a large, physically imposing man who started in his father's iron foundry at fourteen and now owns, through the Spencer Industrial Group, the majority of the mining and timber operations in the regions surrounding Vallam and several further afield, along with a significant portfolio of freight facilities at the Millfield Yards. He does not speak loudly. He speaks once, at a volume appropriate to the room, and expects not to need to repeat himself. This expectation is met in most professional contexts.

His heir, Peter Spencer, twenty-two, returned from the Corda front one year ago. He had volunteered in 1922, served as an artillery officer, been decorated twice, and come back in a condition that anyone who has seen the front would describe without surprise and that Peter himself describes as fine. He is managing a return to the family business's management structure with the specific difficulty of a person who left for the war, spent four years in it, and is now expected to resume a trajectory that was designed for a different person. Lucas Spencer watches this process with a concern he does not know how to express to his son and a patience he is working at, because it does not come naturally.

meta: Upper Aldenmere, Spencer House, a broad stone property built to communicate permanence.

children.title: The Rajiv Family

body.p: The Rajivs are the second-oldest continuous family presence in Vallam, their history in the city predating the Fairbourne dynasty by at least two centuries according to records that the family has maintained and that no external archive fully corroborates. Their origins are in the Cerani-Răvin cultural borderlands, a heritage visible in the family's architecture and the character of their internal culture, which is warm within family lines and precisely calibrated at the boundary.

The family's most discussed aspect is its genetics, present with intensely bright violet eyes and white hair, present from childhood, unconnected to albinism and unexplained by any medical account that the Rajiv family has sought. This trait, which the family calls the clear in their own informal language, a word whose original meaning is not exactly clear (the irony is not lost), appears in perhaps one in three family members, and has done so for as long as the family's own records go back.

The current family head is Fabian Rajiv, seventy-two, who has violet eyes and hair the colour of new snow, and who conducts himself with patience, and knows what is in most rooms before he enters them. He has married children into most of the significant Aldenmere families over the last forty years, with what those who noticed describe as systematic care.

meta: The Old Strand, Rajiv House. A shadowed, angular building of considerable age that sits at the Old Strand's northern extreme, overlooking the water on three sides. It has a quality of presence that people who pass it on the coastal path tend to feel before they can see it clearly.

children.title: Foulere House

body.p: The Fouleres are three generations removed from the docks of the Reach's northern port towns, where the family's original fortune was made in commercial sea trade before Cathair Foulere's grandfather made the pivot to armaments manufacturing that the family has never looked back from. The Foulere Industrial Works, headquartered at a facility in the outer shires east of Vallam, produces a significant share of the Dominion's small-arms ammunition and naval ordnance, a line of business that has become, since 1903, the closest thing the family possesses to a printing press. The Great War has been very good to the Fouleres. They will not say this aloud, they are not unaware of what it implies about them, and they have made their private accommodations with both facts.

The family has a long standing friendly rivalry with the Spencers. The two patriarchs have been to each other's tables, have spoken at the same Chamber of Commerce events, and have, on a couple documented occasions, collaborated on logistics problems to mutual benefit. The Spencers hold the inland resource extraction, and the Fouleres hold the coastal and manufactured goods, and the boundary between those domains has been tested, pushed at, and held through about a decade of courteous hostility. The current patriarch, Cathair Foulere, fifty-one, is an immediately recognisable figure in Aldenmere’s culture. A large man with an extraordinary mane of copper-red hair that has not significantly greyed. He is loud, gregarious, and his handshake is bone-crushing. His son Riordan Foulere, twenty-eight, manages the sea trade arm of the business from the Merchant District offices and is considerably less fun at dinner.

meta: Upper Aldenmere, Foulere House, a broad, red-brick property built with the specific confidence of a family that arrived after the old money and decided this was not a disadvantage. The gateposts are topped with cast-iron anchors. This is not subtle, and it is not meant to be.

children.title: Marie Family

body.p: The Maries built their Aldenmere position on wine, producing an estate wine operation whose quality became, over two generations, the kind of reputation that opens doors in Aldenmere without requiring explanation. The family was comfortably wealthy, socially secure, and entirely unprepared for National Prohibition, which removed the market for their primary product at approximately the same speed that the Great War removed their best remaining export routes to Corda's occupied territories.

Sylvia Marie, thirty-six, took over the family's management five years ago and has spent most of those five years in the process of becoming something more than a vintner's heir with a portfolio problem.

She is diversifying into hospitality with medical goods manufacturing, as well as ownership of many of Vallam’s clinics, including the central hospital. She is stunningly attractive, and the eldest sibling of the Rajiv's current mainline generation, the product of an earlier and differently-named branch of the family. She possesses none of the violet-eyed clarity that marks that bloodline's more visible members.

meta: A townhouse in lower Aldenmere proper, modest by the street's standards, supplemented by a significant collection of estate properties across Vallam's surrounding shires. The family's true holdings are in the rolling country south and west of Vallam.

children.title: Langford Family

body.p: The Langfords are the second significant bastard offshoot of the Fairbourne dynasty in Aldenmere, their line descending from a liaison between the fifth Fairbourne monarch's second son and a Vallam-born parliamentary administrator's daughter in the early eighteenth century, a generation later than the Fairchilds, and a legitimisation that came through a different legal mechanism, which the Langfords and Fairchilds have found no occasion to discuss in their two centuries of proximity. The Langford connection to the main Fairbourne line is sufficiently close and sufficiently documented that the family has, unlike the Fairchilds, held appointed government positions in most generations with advisory roles, departmental chairs, the occasional junior ministry. In 1926, the family's government connections are the most significant thing about them, and they know it, and the two things they have never done are ask for formal recognition of their lineage and behave as though they are not aware of it.

The Langford name is a household one in Vallam primarily through two channels: the Langford Foundation, a charitable body that funds scholarships at both universities, maintains three public reading rooms in the working-class districts, and operates a veterans' support program that is the city's most functional privately-funded equivalent; and Langford & Associates, the city's largest and most politically connected law firm. The current family head, Sir Emery Langford, sixty-six, holds a government advisory position in the Home Ministry that is described in official documents as consultative and functions in practice as something closer to a standing voice in the room where domestic security policy is formed. His daughter Constance Langford, thirty-two, manages the Foundation's operations and is widely considered the more interesting of the two.

meta: Mid-upper Aldenmere, Langford Court, a Georgian property of considerable size whose walls are notable for being the most well-maintained exterior on the entire upper slope.

children.title: Galmier Family

body.p: The Galmiers hold the Wardenship of the Archipelago, a hereditary administrative title established by royal charter in 1763, when the islands' growing commercial importance made it apparent that governing them through the city's standard municipal framework was producing delays, confusion, and revenue losses that the Dominion could not sustain. The Warden holds authority over the archipelago's taxation, its port regulation, its internal legal proceedings up to a specified severity, and the management of its infrastructure, including the ferry services, the causeway, and the lighthouse network that makes the upper bay navigable in the fog conditions that characterise most of autumn and winter. It has a significant amount of practical authority over a collection of communities that generate a meaningful portion of Vallam's seafood supply, its informal shipping trade, and the particular social ecosystem on the islands, close enough to the great city, but far enough away to seem unique.

Warden Pilar Galmier, fifty-seven, has held the position for nineteen years following her mother’s death and has proved considerably more capable in it than her mother’s associates expected when they first assessed her, an assessment she has not forgiven. She is dark-complexioned, and governs the archipelago with the pragmatic attention to function over form that island administration requires.

Her son Aldric Galmier, twenty-nine, manages the Wardenship's mainland interface from the Aldenmere townhouse and the Merchant District administrative office, intermediating the relationship between the archipelago's commercial interests and the city's commercial interests.

meta: Nominally a townhouse in lower Aldenmere, functionally the family spends the majority of its time across the archipelago, specifically on Havelock, where the Galmier administrative compound occupies the island's most defensible high point.

children.title: The Cerani Club Organisation

body.p: The Cerani Club organisation is the oldest substantial criminal enterprise in Vallam, its roots traceable to the early years of Prohibition when a consortium of Cerani-heritage businessmen recognised the opportunity created by the Act's passage and moved quickly to fill the distribution gap in Vallam's wealthiest neighborhoods. At its peak, in 1923–1925, the organisation controlled the majority of alcohol supply into Aldenmere, a significant portion of the upper Merchant District, and a protection arrangement with several Terrace establishments. It held this position for two years before losing most of it.

The event that ended the Cerani Club's dominance, being the killing of its second-in-command (a man known as Clyde Harris) and three senior distribution lieutenants in a series of incidents now referred to, in the criminal community, as the Bad Quarter, was the work of the Vulburrow organisation (see below), which moved with enough speed and enough coordination to significantly disrupt the Cerani Club before it could respond effectively. The Club's current territory is Aldenmere proper and the lower mountain approaches, a position that is comfortable and not expanding. Its leadership knows it is not expanding.

The organisation's effective head is Carlo Benedetti, fifty-five, who manages the Club's legitimate operations. It is a real private members' club with real wine and real food and a real membership, and its criminal ones with an equal hand. He is a Reformist Astralist who attends services at a cathedral in Greenvale monthly and who has, by his own count, not committed a violent act personally since 1918.
He has arranged several since then. He considers the distinction meaningful. His relationship with the Rajiv family is long-standing, mutually beneficial, and does not involve anything written down.

meta: The Cerani Club, Aldenmere, a private club whose public face serves wine to regular members and tells newcomers it does not sell alcohol, this statement being delivered calmly and without apparent irony while wine is visible being consumed at the adjacent tables

children.title: The Corvenza Cartel

body.p: The Corvenza organisation operates Vallam's most comprehensive legitimate-front structure: a trucking and carriage company that genuinely moves goods around the city and its surrounds, a ferry service operating between the mainland and the archipelago, and a marine freight service that runs regular routes between Vallam and several other coastal cities. All of these operations are real, profitable, and useful. They are also the infrastructure through which a significant volume of the city's illicit imports, being alcohol from Răvin, controlled pharmaceuticals from Cerani, goods of various descriptions from several points of origin that the Corvenza Cartel does not advertise, move into and around Vallam.

The cartel is run by the Corvenza family, a Merchant District institution across three generations: the current operational head is Dario Corvenza, forty-eight, whose father established the legitimate freight company in 1897 and whose grandfather was a docker on the same wharf that Dario's ferry service now operates from. Dario Corvenza  is efficient, present, and has the authority that comes from running something that genuinely works. The cartel's primary criminal relationship is with the Răvin Workers' Congress's international networks. A supply connection established in the early years of Prohibition that provides a reliable flow of smuggled alcohol and other goods through the Zodiac route, arriving as legitimate cargo and diverging at the Corvenza yards.

meta: The Merchant District, anchored around a trucking and carriage company, Clover Freight, operating from a yard on the district's southern edge

children.title: Vulburrow Organization

body.p: The Vulburrow organisation is the most numerous criminal enterprise in Vallam in 1926, having expanded rapidly through the Prohibition period into most of the city's working-class and middle-class neighborhoods by providing a simpler service than its competitors. Reliable alcohol at reasonable prices, delivered without excessive complexity. Its leadership model is correspondingly flat, with fewer hierarchical levels than the Cerani Club, more operating cells with direct territory responsibility, and a culture that rewards reliability over loyalty in the more elaborate sense.

It is not the most sophisticated operation in Vallam, and it knows it. The men who lead Vulburrow's cells have come up through the same neighborhoods as their customers, and the organisation's relationship with those spots is accordingly more embedded than the Cerani Club's or the Sycamore Room's. It is also more vulnerable. Its flat structure makes it effective at operating but less effective at responding to the kind of top-level strategic pressure that the Sycamore Room is increasingly applying.

The organisation takes its name from its founder, Thomas Vulburrow, who died in 1923 and is remembered within the organisation with reverence. His successor is Delia Marsh, forty-one, a former Millfield clerk who managed Vulburrow's financial operations from the beginning and took over the organisation's leadership after Thomas's death (in favour of his son Jack Vulburrow) simply by being the person who knew where everything was, how everything worked, and what the relevant people owed. The transition was not challenged all too much outside of Jack’s crew, and people who know Delia Marsh tend to understand immediately why.

meta: Operating across the Confluence, Ironside, and Fenwick, with no single permanent headquarters. Meetings rotate.

children.title: The Sycamore Room

body.p: The Sycamore Room is the newest and most aggressively ambitious criminal organisation in Vallam. It was established approximately four years ago by the Romano family, specifically by Lexy Romano, thirty-seven, and her brother Nico Romano, thirty-four, as the consolidation of several smaller Terrace-area operations into a single entity with unified leadership, unified finances, and a strategy oriented toward long-term dominance rather than the immediate profit that most criminal operations optimise for.

The Romanos came from money. Legitimate, Cerani-origin trade wealth that gave them the initial capital and the social connections to build the Sycamore Room from an actually functioning hotel and nightclub rather than from a back-room arrangement masquerading as one. The club is, by any account, one of the best establishments in Vallam: its performers are exceptional, its wine list is extensive and not fake, and its private rooms, available for the right guests at rates that reflect their privacy rather than their occupancy, are used by people whose presence in the same building as an illegal operation would be legally inconvenient for several of them.

The organisation's members are identifiable to those who know by the purple flower brooch. A stylised sycamore blossom, worn in the lapel, and by the performers whose hair is dyed in the same deep violet.

The Sycamore Room's current operations include a city-wide protection network, the most comprehensive alcohol supply arrangement in the Terrace district, and an expanding network of safehouses and supplier relationships across the surrounding shires that is progressively constricting the other organisations' supply lines. Lexy Romano reads three newspapers every morning and has a map of the city's criminal territory on the wall of her private office that is updated weekly. Nico Romano handles the operations that require physical presence and does not use a map, because he already knows where everything is.

meta: The Sycamore Room, a three-story underground club beneath the Grand Peeress Hotel on the Terrace. The hotel above it is also owned by the same family.

children.title: Black Tally

body.p: The Black Tally presents itself, in the portions of its identity it presents publicly, as a veterans' mutual aid society: men who came back from the Corda front changed, who found that civilian life had no adequate framework for what they had seen and done and endured, who organised around shared experience for mutual support and, eventually, for other purposes. This presentation is not entirely false. The men in the Black Tally did come back from the front, they have changed, and the organisation does provide a community for them that they have not found elsewhere.

The Tally is also something else, and something else is not entirely clear to most of its members. Its lower ranks, what its leadership calls the Counts, know the organisation as a bootlegging and robbery operation with an unusual internal culture with rituals, terminology, a hierarchical structure that has a specifically ceremonial quality to it, and reverence for certain objects and certain individuals that goes beyond what most criminal organisations produce in their members. Its higher ranks, referred to internally as the Old Brass, in a usage that sounds like military slang but isn't quite, know more. The full extent of what the Old Brass know is not communicated to the Counts, in the same way that most cults manage the relationship between what the inner circle understands and what the outer membership is told.

Its founding members are veterans who served in the Corda front's longest-running sections. The areas of continuous engagement, the positions that were held for years at a time. They came back at different points and from different units, without obvious prior connection. They found each other in Vallam and formed the organisation in 1921. The organisation's membership has not significantly decreased, which is notable given its involvement in activities that carry significant mortality rates.

meta: Nominally based in the Confluence and Ironside, with gatherings ( they call them rallies) rotating between three warehouse locations that change on a monthly schedule that members are given at each meeting for the next one only

children.title: The Merr-Boys

body.p: The Merr-Boys are a street gang of subadults, primarily from Ironside and the western Confluence, who have organised around territory, shared identity, and the social infrastructure of a peer group that the city's other institutions have not provided them. The Merr-Boys are not, by Vallam's criminal standards, a significant force, for their activities run to petty theft, minor extortion of local businesses, and the occasional violent confrontation. They hold neutral ground relative to the city's major criminal organisations because they are too small to be worth absorbing and not in anyone's specific territory.

The gang's internal culture centres on a brickyard, which they have been using as a base long enough that several generations of Confluence-area teenagers have passed through it. The current leadership is informal, the Merr-Boys do not have titles,  but centres on Finn Merrit, seventeen, whose family name is the probable origin of the gang's name through a linguistic compression that nobody now living can quite reconstruct. The Merr-Boys' ongoing conflict with the Crofts is largely territorial and largely theatrical in the sense that both sides have enough sense not to actually kill anyone.

meta: The Confluence's eastern edge, centred on an abandoned brickyard off Kiln Street that the gang uses as a base, meeting point, and occasional residence for members who have nowhere else to be

children.title: The Crofts

body.p: The Crofts are the Merr-Boys' primary rival and occasional sparring partner in a more literal sense than most gang rivalries. The gym that serves as their base is a functioning boxing gym with actual training equipment, and a significant number of Crofts members have genuine athletic capability that the gang's culture encourages and that has, in several cases, provided individual members with exits from the gang's trajectory into legitimate sporting careers. The Crofts are predominantly of Cerani heritage, second and third generation, and their connection to the Cerani community of Ironside and the Narrows gives them a cultural identity that the Merr-Boys lack. The Crofts' relationship with the Cerani Club organisation is acknowledged within the gang but not formalised, and the Club does not recruit from the Crofts directly, but several former Crofts members have ended up in the Club's lower-tier operations, and the Club is aware of and comfortable with the Crofts' presence as a territorial stabilising factor in Ironside's western streets.

meta: Ironside's western streets, centred on a boxing gym on Croft Lane, a name that may be the origin of the gang's name or may have been adopted to fit the street; nobody is entirely sure which came first
